headline: Alibaba: cloud growth accelerates to 53% and profit triples, but AI spending pushes free cash flow deeper into the red
takeaway: Revenue rose 10% to RMB271.5 billion and adjusted EBITA jumped 260% as quick-commerce losses shrank and the cloud unit grew 53%. Adjusted EPS of RMB8.10 per ADS was below the RMB11.0 consensus, and capital spending of RMB50.5 billion left free cash flow at minus RMB34.5 billion.
results: Alibaba reported revenue of RMB271.5 billion (US$40.5 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, up 10% from a year earlier. Income from operations rose 443% to RMB29.1 billion and adjusted EBITA rose 260% to RMB32.6 billion. Net income of RMB64.4 billion was inflated by investment gains; non-GAAP net income was RMB19.9 billion, up 92%, or RMB8.10 (US$1.21) per ADS, up 86% but short of the roughly RMB11.0 analysts expected.

The cloud business is now the growth engine. AI cloud and compute revenue rose 53%, revenue from external customers grew 64%, and recurring external revenue grew 67%. AI-related product revenue has grown at triple-digit rates for thirteen straight quarters, and the cloud segment margin improved to 14.5%. In the consumer business, customer management revenue — the fees merchants pay on Taobao and Tmall — fell 5%, or rose 1% excluding a merchant-incentive programme booked as a revenue deduction.

Operating cash flow rose 55% to RMB15.7 billion, but capital expenditure climbed 60% to RMB50.5 billion, so free cash flow was an outflow of RMB34.5 billion against RMB21.8 billion a year ago. Cash and liquid investments stood at RMB487.9 billion (US$72.8 billion).
mgmt: Chief executive Eddie Wu said Alibaba’s full-stack AI capabilities are improving commercialisation, pointing to the acceleration in cloud revenue, the next-generation Zhenwu V900 chip from its T-Head unit, and quick commerce narrowing its losses substantially while keeping market share.

Chief financial officer Toby Xu said the company will keep investing in AI with a focus on return on invested capital while targeting positive free cash flow. The company attributed the jump in capital spending to faster expansion of compute capacity, higher prices for chip components, more CPU capacity for AI agents and the timing of purchases, and said demand is coming from AI labs as well as electric-vehicle, robotics and biotech customers.
view: There are two Alibabas in this report, and the market is pricing only one of them. The consumer Alibaba is a mature marketplace whose core fee income is shrinking on paper and flat in substance, while it spends heavily to defend share in instant delivery against Meituan and JD. The technology Alibaba is the largest cloud provider in China, growing external revenue at 64% with margins that are rising, not falling, as it scales. The second business is the reason the profit line tripled; the first is the reason the revenue line only grew 10%.

The earnings miss deserves less weight than it will get. Consensus numbers for Chinese ADRs are thin and often mix accounting bases, and the trend that matters — adjusted EBITA up 260% and quick-commerce losses falling — is clearly positive. What deserves more weight is cash. Spending RMB50 billion a quarter on data centres when operating cash flow is RMB16 billion means Alibaba is funding AI from its balance sheet. With RMB488 billion of cash and investments it can do that for years, but every yuan spent on servers is a yuan not returned through buybacks, which were the main support for the shares in 2024 and 2025.

The bull case rests on whether Chinese AI demand converts into durable, profitable revenue rather than a capacity race in which chip shortages and export controls set the pace. A cloud margin of 14.5% and growing recurring revenue argue that it is converting. The bear case is that Alibaba is building at peak component prices into a market where Huawei, ByteDance and Tencent are doing the same. At roughly 11 times trailing earnings after a 20% fall in the share price this month, investors are not paying for the cloud optionality; they are paying for the cash pile and a consumer business they no longer trust to grow.
watch: Watch the free cash flow line and management’s promise to turn it positive, the cloud margin as new capacity comes on line, and whether customer management revenue returns to growth once the merchant incentive programme laps.
